findings.issue_text: Changing the global cleanup ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute runs cleanup jobs ten times as often; passes lasting up to 9 minutes can run back-to-back and continuously load the database.
The SQLite literal-ID list is constructed by repeatedly fmt.Sprintf-ing the accumulated string, causing O(n²) copying and gigabytes of allocations for 32,767-ID batches.
Normal cleanup batches log every selected ID at Error level even when no error occurred, creating huge logs, false alerts, and significant logging overhead.

goldens.comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.

The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The SQLite literal-ID list is constructed by repeatedly fmt.Sprintf-ing the accumulated string, causing O(n²) copying and gigabytes of allocations for 32,767-ID batches.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows in xorm_store.go lines 588-592 that the SQLite literal-ID list is built using repeated fmt.Sprintf: `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop. This is indeed O(n²) string concatenation since each iteration copies the entire accumulated string. With batch sizes up to 32,767 (as shown in the test case), this would cause significant memory allocations. While this is a real performance issue in the new code, it's not a correctness bug - the code will still function correctly, just inefficiently. A strings.Builder or similar approach would be more efficient.
